source_refs.note: Chapter 2 exercise (PDF 43-45), solved: 12 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key is printed; X-XII use Chapter 3), 14 short-answer and 3 descriptive questions with model answers. Short (d), the e-i lettering and Short (j) iv carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. The quantum number ‘m’ of a free gaseous atom is associated with:

options.text: the effective volume of the orbital
the spatial orientation of the orbital
the energy of the orbital in the absence of a magnetic field

blocks.explanation: The magnetic quantum number m describes the orientation of an orbital in space (2.5.3); n gives size and energy, ℓ gives shape.

blocks.prompt: II. When 3d subshell is completely filled, the next entering electron goes into:
blocks.explanation: Filling order: … 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s … (n + ℓ rule). 4s is already filled before 3d, so after 3d¹⁰ the next electron enters 4p (e.g. Ga: 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹) (2.7.2).

blocks.prompt: III. Quantum number values for 2p orbitals are:
blocks.explanation: 2 means n = 2 and p means ℓ = 1 (2.5.2). For n = 1, ℓ can only be 0.

blocks.prompt: IV. An electron having the set of values: n = 4, l = 0, m = 0 and s = +1/2 lies in:
blocks.explanation: n = 4 is the fourth shell and ℓ = 0 is an s subshell, so the electron is in 4s.

blocks.prompt: V. The quantum number values for the fourth electron of ⁹₄Be atom are:
blocks.explanation: Be = 1s² 2s². The fourth electron is the second 2s electron: n = 2, ℓ = 0, m = 0 (and s = −½).

blocks.prompt: VI. The correct order of first ionization energies is:
blocks.explanation: He (completely filled 1s, a noble gas) has the highest; F is high (small atom, large nuclear charge); N (half-filled 2p, 1403) is higher than O (spin-paired 2p⁴); Mg (larger, period 3) is lowest (1.7.3, 2.3.2). So He > F > N > O > Mg.

blocks.prompt: VII. A p orbital has a characteristic shape with how many lobes?
blocks.explanation: A p orbital is dumb-bell shaped: two lobes on its axis, with the nucleus between them (2.6.2).

blocks.prompt: VIII. The three p orbitals in a given energy level are oriented:

options.text: Mutually perpendicular to each other along the x, y, and z axes.

blocks.explanation: ℓ = 1 gives m = −1, 0, +1: three orbitals px, py, pz along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to each other (2.6.2).

blocks.prompt: IX. How many d orbitals are there in a given energy level?
X. Which of the following species is predicted to have the highest bond order?
blocks.explanation: From MOT (Chapter 3, 3.6.1): bond order = (bonding − antibonding electrons)/2. N₂ = 3, O₂ = 2, F₂ = 1, Ne₂ = 0.

blocks.prompt: XI. Which of the following species has a zero bond order according to MOT?
blocks.explanation: He₂: σ1s² σ*1s², bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0, so He₂ does not form (Chapter 3, 3.6.1). H₂⁺ = (1 − 0)/2 = ½; He₂⁺ = (2 − 1)/2 = ½; He₂²⁺ = (2 − 0)/2 = 1.

blocks.prompt: XII. Which of the following molecular geometries has bond angles of approximately 120°?
blocks.explanation: Three bond pairs and no lone pair around the central atom give a trigonal planar shape with 120° angles, e.g. BF₃ (Chapter 3, 3.3.2). Tetrahedral is 109.5°; pyramidal 107°; bent less than 120° or 109.5°.

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. There are three orientations of p-orbital due to three values of magnetic quantum number. Justify it.
blocks.explanation: For a p subshell ℓ = 1, and m takes (2ℓ + 1) = 3 values: −1, 0, +1. Each value is one orbital with its own orientation in space: px, py and pz along the x, y and z axes, mutually perpendicular and of equal energy (degenerate).

blocks.prompt: b. Size of Mg is bigger than Al, but ionization energy of Mg is more than that of Al. Why?
blocks.explanation: Mg (3s²) has a completely filled, stable 3s subshell. Al (3s² 3p¹) loses a single 3p electron, which has higher energy than 3s and is shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily. Hence IE of Mg > IE of Al.

blocks.prompt: c. ‘I₃’ of Mg is much bigger than its ‘I₂’. Justify.
blocks.explanation: Mg = 2, 8, 2. I₁ and I₂ remove the two 3s electrons of the outer shell. I₃ removes an electron from the second shell (2p⁶ of the stable neon core), which is much closer to the nucleus and less shielded, and from a positive Mg²⁺ ion. So there is a large jump: I₃ ≫ I₂ (2.3.2).

blocks.prompt: d. Among the elements Li, K, Ca, S and Kr which one has the lowest first ionization energy? Which has the highest first ionization.
blocks.explanation:
Lowest: K, an alkali metal in period 4 (large atom, one 4s electron, heavily shielded).
Highest: Kr, a noble gas with a completely filled 4s² 4p⁶ shell.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The second question is cut short: “Which has the highest first ionization.” ends without the word “energy” and without a question mark; it means “Which has the highest first ionization energy?”

blocks.prompt: e. Consider the electronic configuration of the potassium atom (atomic number 19).
blocks.explanation: This is the stem of parts (f) and (g) below. Potassium has 19 electrons in four shells: K 2, L 8, M 8, N 1.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Items e to i are printed with their own letters although they are parts of two questions: e is the stem of f (i) and g (ii), and h (i) and i (ii) are the two parts of one question about element X.

blocks.prompt: f. (i) Write the full electronic configuration of potassium using the s, p, d, f notation.
blocks.explanation: ₁₉K = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹

blocks.prompt: g. (ii) Explain why the 4s subshell is filled before the 3d subshell in potassium, even though the principal quantum number of the 3d subshell is lower.
blocks.explanation: By the Aufbau principle subshells fill in order of increasing energy, judged by (n + ℓ): 4s = 4 + 0 = 4, 3d = 3 + 2 = 5. The lower (n + ℓ) means lower energy, so the 19th electron enters 4s, not 3d.

blocks.prompt: h. i) An atom of element X has an atomic number of 17 and a mass number of 35. Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in this atom.
blocks.explanation:
Protons = Z = 17
Neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18
Electrons = 17 (neutral atom)

blocks.prompt: i. (ii) If this element forms an ion with a charge of -1, how many protons, neutrons, and electrons will be present in the ion?
blocks.explanation:
X⁻ (like Cl⁻) gains one electron; the nucleus does not change:
Protons = 17
Neutrons = 18
Electrons = 17 + 1 = 18

blocks.prompt:
j. In the ground state of mercury ₈₀Hg:
i. How many electrons occupy atomic orbitals with n = 3?
ii. How many electrons occupy 4d atomic orbitals?
iii. How many electrons occupy 4pz atomic orbital?
iv. How many electrons have spin “up” (s = -½)?
blocks.explanation:
₈₀Hg = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶ 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁶ 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s²
i. n = 3: 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ = 18 electrons (= 2n²)
ii. 4d: 10 electrons
iii. 4pz: 2 electrons (one orbital holds at most two)
iv. All 80 electrons are paired (every subshell is full), so half have spin up: 40 electrons.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part iv prints spin “up” as s = -½. In the chapter (2.7 and Table 2.6) the up arrow (↑) is s = +½ and the down arrow (↓) is s = −½. The answer, 40, is the same either way because all the electrons of Hg are paired.

blocks.prompt:
k. The successive ionization energies for an unknown element are
I₁ = 896 kJ/mol, I₂ = 1752 kJ/mol
I₃ = 14,807 kJ/mol, I₄ = 17,948 kJ/mol
To which family in the periodic table, does the unknown element most likely belong?
blocks.explanation: The big jump is between I₂ (1752) and I₃ (14,807), about 8 times. So the first two electrons are removed from the valence shell and the third comes from an inner shell: the element has 2 valence electrons. It belongs to group 2, the alkaline earth metals (the values fit beryllium).

blocks.prompt:
l. Consider the following ionization energies for aluminum:
Al(g) → Al⁺(g) + e⁻   I₁ = 580 kJ/mol
Al⁺(g) → Al²⁺(g) + e⁻   I₂ = 1815 kJ/mol
Al²⁺(g) → Al³⁺(g) + e⁻   I₃ = 2740 kJ/mol
Al³⁺(g) → Al⁴⁺(g) + e⁻   I₄ = 11,600 kJ/mol
(i) Account for the trend in the values of the ionization energies.
(ii) Explain the large increase between I₃ and I₄.
(iii) List the four aluminum ions given in order of increasing size, and explain your ordering.
blocks.explanation:
(i) Each electron is removed from a more positive ion; the same nuclear charge (+13) holds fewer electrons, repulsion falls and the ion shrinks, so every next electron is harder to remove: I₁ < I₂ < I₃ < I₄.
(ii) Al = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹. I₁, I₂, I₃ remove the three valence electrons (3p¹, 3s²). I₄ removes an electron from the inner second shell (2p⁶, noble gas core), much closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so I₄ jumps (11,600).
(iii) Al⁴⁺ < Al³⁺ < Al²⁺ < Al⁺. Fewer electrons with the same 13 protons means less repulsion and stronger pull per electron, so the more positive ion is smaller; Al³⁺ and Al⁴⁺ have also lost the whole third shell.

blocks.prompt:
m. (a) State the general order of filling orbitals up to the 4p subshell.
(b) Explain why the 4s subshell is filled before the 3d subshell, according to the Aufbau principle.
blocks.explanation:
(a) 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p
(b) Subshells fill in order of increasing energy, given by (n + ℓ): 4s has 4 + 0 = 4 and 3d has 3 + 2 = 5. Lower (n + ℓ) means lower energy, so 4s fills first. (When (n + ℓ) is equal, as for 3d and 4p (both 5), the lower n, 3d, fills first.)

blocks.prompt: n. Draw the orbital box diagram for the valence electrons of a phosphorus atom (atomic number 15), ensuring that your diagram adheres to Hund’s rule and the Pauli Exclusion Principle.
blocks.explanation:
₁₅P = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³; valence electrons 3s² 3p³.
Draw one box for 3s and three boxes for 3p (3px, 3py, 3pz):
3s: [↑↓]   3p: [↑] [↑] [↑]
Pauli: the two 3s electrons have opposite spins. Hund: the three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals with the same spin (3 unpaired electrons, a half-filled 3p subshell).

blocks.prompt: Q.3 What are quantum numbers? Describe briefly principal and spin quantum numbers.
blocks.explanation:
Quantum numbers are the set of numbers that describe the size, energy, shape and orientation in space of an orbital and the spin of an electron in it. Schrödinger's wave equation gives three (n, ℓ, m); the fourth (s) is for spin. No two electrons in an atom have all four the same (Pauli).
Principal quantum number (n):
1. Values 1, 2, 3, 4 … (shells K, L, M, N …), corresponding to Bohr's orbit number.
2. It describes the size and energy of the orbital: the larger n, the farther the electron from the nucleus, the larger the orbital and the higher the energy (less tightly bound).
3. A shell is the collection of orbitals with the same n; it holds at most 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32) and has n subshells and n² orbitals.
Spin quantum number (s):
1. An electron spins on its own axis; a spinning charge produces a magnetic field, so the electron behaves like a small magnet.
2. Two spins are possible: clockwise, s = +½ (↑), and anticlockwise, s = −½ (↓).
3. Three quantum numbers describe an orbital; the fourth distinguishes the two electrons in it. An orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins (e.g. He: 1, 0, 0, +½ and 1, 0, 0, −½).

blocks.prompt: Q4. Draw the shapes of s, p and d-orbitals. Justify these by keeping in view the azimuthal and magnetic quantum numbers.
blocks.explanation:
The azimuthal quantum number ℓ (0 to n − 1) gives the shape; the magnetic quantum number m (−ℓ … 0 … +ℓ) gives the number of orbitals (2ℓ + 1) and their orientations.
s orbital (ℓ = 0, m = 0): one orbital, spherical. Draw a sphere centred on the nucleus at the origin of the x, y, z axes; electron density is the same in all directions. 2s is a larger sphere than 1s (draw 2s as a bigger sphere with a smaller one inside).
p orbitals (ℓ = 1, m = −1, 0, +1): three orbitals, dumb-bell shaped. Draw each as two lobes meeting at the nucleus: px along the x axis, py along the y axis, pz along the z axis; the three are mutually perpendicular and of equal energy.
d orbitals (ℓ = 2, m = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2): five orbitals, mostly double dumb-bell (cloverleaf):
- dxy, dxz, dyz: four lobes lying in the xy, xz and yz planes, between the axes.
- dx²−y²: four lobes along the x and y axes.
- dz²: two lobes along the z axis with a doughnut-shaped ring in the xy plane.
So the three values of m for ℓ = 1 justify three p orientations, and the five values for ℓ = 2 justify five d orientations; ℓ = 0 has one value, so the s orbital has no directional orientation (spherical).

blocks.prompt: Q.5 What do you mean by successive ionization energies? How the electronic shell structure of magnesium (Mg) is derived from the successive ionization energies?
blocks.explanation:
Successive ionization energies: the energies needed to remove the electrons of an atom one by one, in sequence, until only the nucleus is left:
X → X⁺ + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁
X⁺ → X²⁺ + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₂
X²⁺ → X³⁺ + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₃ …
Each is larger than the one before, because the electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.
Shell structure of Mg (12 electrons): when log₁₀ of the twelve successive ionization energies is plotted against the number of electrons removed:
1. Electrons 1 and 2 need low energy: they are in the outermost (third) shell.
2. A large jump comes at the 3rd electron: after the two outer electrons, the next is removed from a shell much closer to the nucleus.
3. Electrons 3 to 10 show a gradual rise: eight electrons in the second shell.
4. A second, even bigger jump comes at the 11th electron; electrons 11 and 12 come from the first, innermost shell next to the nucleus.
The two large jumps show three shells: Mg = 2, 8, 2 (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²).
